title: Chapter 4: Talking Back: Input and Type Conversion
video_title: Python Chapter 4: Talking Back, Input and Type Conversion
summary: Asha's receipt gave every customer the same order. Follow her as she makes it ask the customer with input(), and converts the answers with int() and float() so the program can calculate. Then watch her add a change calculator with an AI assistant at all six stages, debugging with the exact error and catching two AI mistakes by testing.

segments.say: Remember Asha's receipt from Chapter 3? Neat columns, two decimal places. Very professional.
But there is a problem. Every customer gets the same order, two teas and a sandwich.
Omar wants three teas? Asha has to open the code and change it. That is not how a real cafe program works.

visual.heading: Today's mission: a receipt that asks

segments.say: So here is today's mission. The program asks the customer three questions.
Then it prints the receipt for that order, and only that order.
Different answers, different receipt, and not one line of code changes. Let's build it, piece by piece.

scenes.title: The idea: every answer is text
scenes.direction: Teach input() with the diagram, then the conversion table, then the waiter analogy. Then a quiz, then a breather.

visual.heading: input() gives back text
visual.label: The idea
body: `input()` shows a question, waits for Enter, and gives back what was typed.
visual.pre:
input("How many teas? ")
        |
        v
  The terminal shows:  How many teas? _
  The user types 3 and presses Enter
        |
        v
  input() gives back the string "3", not the number 3

segments.say: Here is the big idea. The function input shows a question, and then it waits.
The user types an answer and presses Enter. Then input gives back exactly what they typed.
And here is the important part. The answer is always a string. Even when the user types the digit 3, you get the text 3, not the number.

visual.heading: One conversion for each type
visual.label: The idea

segments.say: To calculate with an answer, you convert it. Converting means making a new value of another type.
Int makes a whole number. The text 3 becomes the number 3.
Float makes a decimal number, for prices like 4.25.
And str goes the other way. It turns a number into text.

visual.heading: Like a waiter's order slip
visual.label: Analogy
items: The waiter writes every order on a paper slip: that is `input()`.
The kitchen needs numbers to add up: conversion reads the slip.
Unlike a person, a conversion cannot guess. "two" instead of "2" stops it with an error.

segments.say: Think of a waiter. Every order goes onto a paper slip. That is input: everything arrives as writing.
The kitchen cannot add up slips. It needs numbers. Conversion reads the slip and writes the number.
But unlike a person, a conversion cannot guess. If the slip says the word two, instead of the digit, it stops with an error.

visual.question: The user types `3` and presses Enter. What does `input()` give back?
visual.explain: `input()` always gives back a string, even when the user types digits.

segments.say: Quick check. The user types 3 and presses Enter. What does input give back?

after.say: B. The string 3. Input always gives back text.

items: `input()` asks and waits.
Every answer is a string.
`int()` and `float()` turn text into numbers.

scenes.title: Step 2: Every answer is text
scenes.direction: Use type() to prove the answer is a string, then let the learner predict the repeat.

visual.heading: Step 2: What type is the answer?

segments.say: Step 2. Asha asks how many teas, and the user types 3.
Line 3 prints the answer and its type, with the type function from Chapter 2.
Line 4 multiplies the answer by 2. Remember the big idea about answers.

after.say: Line 3 shows class str. The answer is a string.

scenes.title: Step 3: Convert with int()
scenes.direction: Teach the inside-out order of int(input()), then the prediction.

visual.heading: Step 3: Turn the answer into a number

segments.say: Step 3. The fix is to put input inside int.
Python works from the inside out. First, input gives back the string 3. Then int turns it into the number 3.
Line 4 checks the type again. Line 5 calculates the cost, with two decimal places.

ask.question: The user types 3. What does line 5 print now?

after.say: Line 4 shows class int: a whole number.
So line 5 really calculates. 3 teas cost 10.50.

scenes.title: Step 4: Convert with float()
scenes.direction: Two questions, two conversions. Teach the rule for choosing, then predict the last line.

visual.heading: Step 4: Prices need float()

segments.say: Step 4. Remember the price stored as text in Chapter 3? You were promised a way to turn text into a number. Here it is: float. A price can have a decimal point, like 4.25, so line 2 uses float.
A count is always whole, so line 3 uses int.
Here is the rule. Use int for counts, and float for amounts of money.
Line 4 multiplies, and line 5 prints the total.

ask.question: The user types 4.25, then 2. What does line 5 print?

after.say: Two questions, one after the other.
Then: 2 cakes cost 8.50.

scenes.title: Step 5: What each conversion accepts
scenes.direction: Teach the general rules, ask about two lines, then reveal the surprises. Quiz, then a breather.

visual.heading: Step 5: Conversions without input()

segments.say: Step 5. Conversions also work on values you write in the code. No questions this time.
Remember the table: int makes a whole number from text, and str turns a number into text.

after.say: Line 2: the text 12 becomes the number 12, plus 1 is 13.
Line 7: str turns 4 into text, so plus can join it to the word teas.
Line 3: float turns the text 2.5 into a number, so times 2 gives 5.0.
Now the surprises. Line 4: float accepts text without a decimal point, and adds point 0.
Line 5: int on 3.9 gives 3. It cuts off the part after the point. It does not round!
And line 6: int ignores spaces at the start and the end of the text.

visual.heading: Step 5: a number is not text

segments.say: Careful with one difference. Int accepts the number 3.9, and cuts it down to 3.
But the text 3.9, in quotation marks, is not a whole number. Int stops with a Value Error, instead of cutting off the decimals.
So for answers with a decimal point, use float.

visual.question: What does `int(7.8)` give?
visual.explain: `int()` cuts off the part after the point. It does not round.

segments.say: Quick check. What does int of 7.8 give?

after.say: A, 7. Int cuts off the decimals. It does not round.

items: `int()` for counts, `float()` for money.
Python works out `int(input(...))` from the inside out.
`int()` cuts off decimals.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: the exact error
visual.label: Before you start
items: When a program stops, copy the full error and the code.
Ask for the cause first, and only then for the smallest fix.
Never paste passwords or private data. You are responsible for the code you use.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is debugging with the exact error.
When a program stops, copy the full error message and the code into your prompt.
Ask for the cause first. Only then ask for the smallest fix. A fix you do not understand will break again.
And the safety habits from Chapter 1 still apply.

visual.heading: Plan: the questions and their types

messages.text: I am a beginner learning input(). After the receipt, I want to ask how much the customer paid and print the change. Do not write code yet. List the steps, and say which type the answer needs.

1. Ask `Amount paid? ` with `input()`.
2. Convert the answer with `float()`, because money can have decimals.
3. Subtract the bill from the amount paid.
4. Print the change with `.2f`.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha describes the change feature, and asks which type the answer needs. No code yet.
The AI lists four steps. Step 2 converts with float, because money can have decimals. That matches the rule from step 4.

visual.heading: Write it yourself, then explain it

messages.text: I wrote the question line myself. Do not change it. Explain the order in which Python works it out, and the type after each step.

1. `input()` shows `Amount paid? ` and gives back the text the customer types, such as `"30"`.
2. `float()` turns that text into the number 30.0.
3. The name `paid` now refers to 30.0, a `float`.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes the question line herself, and asks the AI to explain it from the inside out.
Input first, then float, then the name. Exactly the order you learned in step 3.

visual.heading: Generate: compare with an AI version

messages.text: Now write the whole change program, so I can compare it with mine. The bill is 22.5. Use the names to_pay, paid and change. If I type 30, tell me exactly what it prints.
Here is the program. If you type 30, it prints `Change: 7.50`.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks the AI for the whole program, to compare it with hers.
The AI promises: type 30, and it prints change 7.50. It sounds sure.
Check every line before you trust it.

ask.question: The AI says that typing 30 prints `Change: 7.50`. Is it right?

after.say: No! Its line 3 has input, but no float. The answer stays text. Let's see what happens when Asha tests it.

visual.heading: Test: try the AI's own answers

messages.text: Before I trust it, give me three answers to test it with, and what each one should print.
I tried your first answer, 30. It did not print the change. It showed the question, then stopped with an error.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks for three test answers, with the result each one should give.
The AI suggests 30, 22.5, and 25.50.
She tries the first one. The program shows the question, and then it stops with an error.

visual.heading: Debug: the exact error, the cause first

messages.text: Here is the code and the full error. I typed 30. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.
Line 4 subtracts a number from text. `input()` on line 3 gives back a string, and the code never converts it. Put `float()` around `input()`:
I ran the fix and typed 30:

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. This is today's skill. Asha pastes the code, her answer and the full error. A Type Error on line 4.
She asks for the cause first. The AI explains: input gives back a string, and you cannot subtract a number from text. The fix is float.
She runs the fix and types 30. Change: 7.50. Now the promise is true.

visual.heading: Improve: test every suggestion

messages.text: Review my program. Suggest at most two improvements, each with one reason. Do not change what it prints for any answer.

1. Rename `paid` to `amount_paid`, so a reader knows what the number is.
2. Use `int()` instead of `float()`. Customers usually pay with whole notes, and whole numbers are simpler.
Suggestion 2 fails your own test answer, 25.50. I tried it:

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for at most two improvements that do not change the output.
Suggestion 1, a clearer name, helps. Suggestion 2 says: use int, because customers pay with whole notes.
Asha uses the AI's own test answer, 25.50. Int cannot read text with a decimal point. Value Error! The AI was wrong again.

visual.heading: The finished change line

segments.say: So Asha keeps suggestion 1 only: the clearer name, amount paid, with float.
She tests it with 25.50. Change: 3.00. The AI helped at every stage, and Asha checked every answer.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistakes 1 and 2 call back to the AI stages. Mistakes 3 and 4 are spot-it questions on rules taught earlier.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: an answer you did not convert

segments.say: Mistake 1 is the same kind of mistake as the AI's first one. Line 2 reads the answer, but never converts it.
So line 3 tries to add 1 to the text 3, and Python stops with a Type Error. With plus, the message says can only concatenate. With minus, it said unsupported operand. The cause is the same.
The fix: convert the answer where you read it, with int around input.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: int() for a decimal answer

segments.say: Mistake 2 is the AI's second mistake. Int for a price. The user types 4.25, and int cannot read it.
The message says invalid literal with base 10. A literal is the text Python tried to read, and base 10 means normal digits. The fix: use float for money.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Now you try. The user answers with a word. Remember the waiter's slip from the idea section.

ask.question: The user types `two`. What happens on line 2?

after.say: A Value Error. Int cannot guess that the word two means 2.
after.heading: Mistake 3: an answer that is not a number

after.say: For now, make the prompt say what to type. In later chapters, you will learn to check an answer before you convert it.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: One more. Count the brackets on line 2, like Asha learned in Chapter 1.

after.say: A closing bracket. Int and input each open one, so the line needs two closing brackets.
after.heading: Mistake 4: a missing closing bracket

after.say: This is a syntax error, so the program never even asks the question.

visual.question: Which line reads a price that can have decimals?
visual.explain: `float()` reads text with a decimal point, such as 4.25.

segments.say: Quick check. Which line reads a price that can have decimals?

after.say: C. Float around input. Option A keeps text, and option B fails for 4.25.

items: Convert an answer where you read it.
`float()` for money, `int()` for counts.
Count your brackets.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: `input()` shows a prompt and gives back the answer as a string.
`int()` makes a whole number, `float()` a decimal number, `str()` text.
Python works out `int(input(...))` from the inside out.
`int()` cuts off decimals. It cannot read `"4.25"` or `"two"`.
Give AI the code, your answer and the full error. Ask for the cause first.

segments.say: Let's recap.
Input shows a prompt, and gives back the answer as a string.
Int makes a whole number, float a decimal number, and str makes text.
Python works out int of input from the inside out.
Int cuts off decimals, and it cannot read 4.25 or the word two.
And with AI: paste the code, your answer and the full error, and ask for the cause first.

visual.question: `tea_count = input("How many teas? ")` and the user types `2`. What does `print(tea_count * 3)` show?
visual.explain: The answer is the string `"2"`, so `* 3` repeats it three times.

segments.say: One last check. The answer is not converted, and the user types 2. What does tea count times 3 show?

after.say: B. 222. The answer is text, so times 3 repeats it. Convert first!
